problem: Open-vocabulary mobile manipulation in real homes performs poorly (the NeurIPS 2023 OVMM challenge winner got 33%), even though VLMs, navigation and grasping primitives are each mature. Errors in the individual components compound, and prior systems are closed, trained in-domain, or tested only in simulation or controlled settings.
motivation: General-purpose home robots need zero-shot pick-and-drop on arbitrary novel objects in unseen homes without retraining. The authors argue the bottleneck is not any single model but the nuanced integration of Open Knowledge models (trained on public data) with robot primitives. So they take a systems-first approach and study what matters in the real world.
key_idea: Combine off-the-shelf open-knowledge models (OWL-ViT/CLIP/SAM semantic voxel memory, AnyGrasp + LangSam grasping) with simple navigation and drop heuristics in a linear state machine on a Hello Robot Stretch. The result is a training-free pick-and-drop system that works in novel homes after only a ~1-minute iPhone scan.
insight: Pre-trained VLMs and grasp models work zero-shot on a real robot, but performance depends heavily on details: the choice of grasp model, heuristics for horizontal grasps, and navigation scoring that puts the robot at arm's length. The ablation shows AnyGrasp is almost 50% better in relative terms than the next-best grasper (a top-down heuristic), which itself beats Open Graspness and Contact-GraspNet, and that VoxelMap is slightly better and much lower-variance than CLIP-Fields and USA-Net. Cleaning up the environment cuts navigation error from 15% to 4% and manipulation error from 25% to 13%, so ambiguity, clutter and query wording (the 'incantation' sensitivity of VLMs) dominate failures. Multiplicative error accumulation with no error recovery is a core weakness.
method: Home scan and VoxelMap: an iPhone (Record3D) scan gives posed RGB-D frames. OWL-ViT (queries from the ScanNet200 labels) detects objects on every frame and SAM refines the boxes to masks. Masks are back-projected into a point cloud with CLIP embeddings, voxelized at 5 cm, and each voxel stores the detector-confidence-weighted average CLIP vector.

Language querying: the query is encoded with the CLIP text encoder and the voxel with the maximum dot product is the target. 'A on B' is treated as 'A near B' by taking top-10 A points and top-50 B points and choosing the A point with the smallest pairwise L2 distance.

Navigation: an A* planner runs on a 10 cm 2D obstacle grid derived from the VoxelMap, with unexplored cells non-navigable and a 20 cm inflation radius. An s3 obstacle-proximity term acts as a heuristic, giving Voronoi-like paths. The goal pose minimises s = s1 + 8 s2 + 8 s3 (distance to the object, arm's-length band, obstacle clearance) and faces the object.

Grasp perception and filtering: after arriving, the head RGB-D image is captured and AnyGrasp proposes collision-free parallel-jaw grasps. LangSam masks the target and only grasps projecting inside the mask are kept. The best grasp maximises S - θ^4/10, which favours horizontal grasps that are robust to hand-eye calibration error.

Grasp execution: a pre-grasp approach follows p-0.2a, p-0.08a, p-0.04a, p with progressively smaller steps, then a closed-loop gripper close. The arm is retracted and the wrist rotated so the object is tucked over the robot body.

Drop heuristic: the drop target is navigated to with the same VoxelMap. LangSam segments the drop location in the head point cloud, which is aligned to the robot frame and floor. The drop height is 0.2 plus the max z of points with 0<=x<=x_m and |y-y_m|<0.1. This handles concave receptacles such as sinks, bins and bags.
State machine: a fixed linear chain (navigate to object, grasp, navigate to goal, drop) with no error detection or retry.

setting.backbone: Modular pretrained open-knowledge models (frozen): OWL-ViT, CLIP, SAM, LangSam, AnyGrasp; GPT-4V only to generate object queries in the experiment protocol
setting.training_data: none (training-free); uses pre-trained models as-is (e.g. AnyGrasp trained on GraspNet-1B)
setting.observation: iPhone-scanned posed RGB-D (Record3D) for mapping; Stretch head RealSense RGB-D at grasp time; robot odometry
setting.action_space: Planned 2D A* base path to a target pose, then a scripted end-effector pre-grasp trajectory (grasp pose from AnyGrasp) and a heuristic drop pose
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration: a manual iPhone scan of the home is required before operation, and the map is static. Objects the semantic memory cannot localise are filtered out before the pick-and-drop trials.

numbers.eval_set_note: Cleaned-up, decluttered homes with ambiguous or adversarial objects excluded; the uncleaned-home success rate is given only via an unexpanded macro (\homesuccessrate) in the provided text.
numbers.backbone: OWL-ViT + CLIP + SAM + LangSam + AnyGrasp on Hello Robot Stretch
numbers.extra: Requires iPhone pre-scan; evaluation after cleanup rounds (improved queries, declutter, removal of adversarial objects); unseen NYC homes

numbers_note: The headline success rate over the 10 unseen cluttered homes is an unexpanded LaTeX macro (\homesuccessrate) in the provided text, so it is not reported here. The abstract only says '82%' for clean settings and 'nearly 1.8x' the prior work. Module ablation results (VoxelMap vs CLIP-Fields vs USA-Net; AnyGrasp vs alternatives) appear only in figures, and per-trial outcomes are in the appendix table.
results: OK-Robot runs zero-shot in 10 unseen real homes and reports nearly 1.8x the success rate of prior OVMM work (the NeurIPS 2023 challenge winner UniTeam reached 33%). Its success rate rises to 82.4% in cleaner, decluttered environments. It was also reproduced in larger homes in Pittsburgh and Fremont. The leading failure causes are wrong object retrieval from memory (9.3%), difficult grasp poses (8.0%) and robot hardware (7.5%).
limitations: The semantic memory and obstacle map are static after the initial scan, so the system cannot handle dynamic homes. A manual pre-scan is also required.

Errors accumulate multiplicatively with no failure detection or retry. Grasping uses single-view grasp proposals and open-loop trajectories, and struggles with flat objects. It is also limited by the Stretch payload (1 kg) and reach, and by hardware miscalibration.
VLM retrieval is sensitive to query wording and ambiguous objects, and there is no user interaction to disambiguate.
